title: How to Teach the Perfect Storm Class, Slow Down to Speed Up
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: Dr Dario Emanuele addresses the class where every negative factor aligns, what he calls the Perfect Storm, and the pressure teachers feel to keep delivering curriculum content to students who are not ready to receive it. Drawing on Lovell and Dowley's Classroom Management Handbook, he argues that behaviour is a subject that must be taught explicitly, and sets out a five-level Hierarchy of a Good Learning Environment in which behaviour is the foundation for listening, understanding, good work and independent practice. He recounts a disastrous lesson from his NQT year, carefully planned but wasted because the class was not listening, and the colleague's advice that saved his career: if students are not ready for a topic, do not teach it. He criticises school leaders for prioritising pace over understanding and urges teachers to adjust the scheme of learning, trading curriculum time for behaviour time and foundations. He meets the assessment objection head-on, arguing that a rushed disruptive class will fail anyway while a slowed-down class at least learns what it was taught.
points: Emanuele reframes behaviour as a curriculum in its own right, taught explicitly through the school's behaviour policy as its 'scheme of learning'.
His Hierarchy of a Good Learning Environment makes each level conditional on the one below, so a Perfect Storm class stuck at behaviour cannot be pushed into understanding.
He says teachers of such classes must accept losing curriculum time to behaviour time, and that pushing too fast yields no content learning, no behaviour learning and teacher burnout.
He criticises school leaders for rarely telling teachers they may pause content, and for prioritising pace over understanding.
On assessment, he argues a disruptive class rushed through content will fail anyway, whereas slowing down produces solid learning, a better environment and student respect.
quotes: At the start of every academic year, I go through the same ritual. I sit down with my class lists and start analysing. I look at the sets (low, middle, high), the SEN needs, the history of the class, and who comes from a lower set or higher set.

Their principle is simple but profound: Behaviour is a subject like any other. It must be taught explicitly, following a “scheme of learning” (your school’s behavior policy). If the students are not taught how to behave, how can we expect them to do it?

If you are teaching a “Perfect Storm” class, your class is often stuck at step #1. This means you have to accept a hard truth: You will lose curriculum time to behaviour time. If you don’t, the consequences can be really bad.
I remember sitting with my mentor, looking at a disastrous lesson. I had planned it carefully. The worksheets were scaffolded; the activities were engaging.

I felt like I was failing because I wasn’t “getting through the content.” I felt forced to plow ahead because the calendar said we had to be on Unit 3, even though the class hadn’t mastered Unit 1. The result was chaos.
It frustrates me that school leaders rarely tell us this, and this seems more like a secret rule no one talks about. They often seem to prioritise pace over understanding.

If you plow through the curriculum with a disruptive class, they will still fail the assessment because they weren’t listening, or they didn’t understand the foundational concepts. But in that scenario, everyone is miserable.
